Introduction
ASB Chair Dame Therese Walsh (left)  
and Chief Executive Officer Vittoria Shortt
In July 2023, the world experienced some of its hottest 
days on record. Here in Aotearoa, extreme weather events 
like the Wairoa floods showed us our most vulnerable 
communities continue to be most impacted by the effects 
of climate change. From flooding to coastal erosion, 
the impacts of a changing climate are wide ranging and 
will require both the public and private sectors to work 
together on New Zealand’s adaptation response. We 
are heartened to see the Government developing an 
adaptation framework, and look forward to working with 
them and other stakeholders to ensure this becomes 
an enduring piece of legislation to guide New Zealand’s 
adaptation response.
Globally, the climate challenge is increasing in both scope 
and complexity. The World Economic Forum ranks the 
top 10 global risks by severity over the short and long 
term, and it paints a stark picture. The short-term (two 
year) view reflects familiar risks – mis- and disinformation, 
economic downturn, inflation, with just two climate 
risks in the mix: extreme weather events and pollution. 
Look ahead a decade, and projections show we could be 
facing new challenges – critical change to Earth systems; 
biodiversity loss and ecosystem collapse; natural resource 
shortages. 
Given these global and local challenges, the introduction 
of mandatory climate reporting for eligible financial 
institutions in Aotearoa New Zealand is timely. ASB began 
voluntarily reporting on our climate response efforts 
in 2022. We’ve chosen to combine our first mandatory 
climate statement with a Sustainability Report to showcase 
the bank's broader approach to sustainability. While the 
bulk of this report is necessarily focused on climate, we 
also wanted to present the full picture of our progress 
across the social and financial strands of our purpose. The 
first two sections of this report provide a voluntary update 
and do not form part of the mandatory climate statement.
ASB is committed to supporting Aotearoa’s climate 
transition. Financed Emissions (emissions financed by 
lending and/or investments) are our most material source 
of business activity emissions. We believe the allocation 
of capital can be one of the biggest levers for emissions 
mitigation and climate adaptation which will support 
Aotearoa New Zealand in its transition to a lower-emissions 
economy. ASB is also progressively setting sector-level 
Financed Emissions reduction targets in line with the goals 
of the New Zealand Government’s emissions budget.
Our climate strategy is directly linked to our purpose of 
accelerating progress for all New Zealanders. Supporting 
our customers to transition to low-emissions is the first 
of our three climate priorities, and this report outlines 
the work we are doing to support customers across our 
corporate, business, rural, and personal banking portfolios.
When it comes to financial progress, protecting our 
customers from fraud and scams remains a critical focus. 
This year we spent almost $100 million with the aim of 
protecting ASB and its customers against fraud, scams, 
financial and cyber crime. Since we launched our 24/7 
fraud line in February, our overnight team has supported 
customers with more than 6,000 calls outside of business 
hours.
With housing supply and affordability continuing to be 
an important social issue in New Zealand, we have taken 
actions to support improving housing outcomes, including 
for Ma¯ori who are identified as being disproportionately 
affected by the country's housing shortage. In November, 
we launched the $500 million Accelerated Housing Fund, 
which aims to reduce financing hurdles experienced by 
residential developers, social housing investors and for 
Ma¯ori housing, by adjusting key lending metrics and 
criteria. Under the fund, $100 million has already been 
committed.
Finally, thank you to our people, customers and 
stakeholders for continuing to support sustainability at 
ASB. Supporting Aotearoa New Zealand to transition to a 
low-emissions economy is not only good for people and the 
planet, it simply makes good business sense – presenting 
significant opportunities for innovation and to improve 
outcomes for future generations. Our purpose is ultimately 
about people – we want to accelerate progress for all New 
Zealanders, financially, environmentally and socially. Our 
sustainability agenda is absolutely key to delivering this.

Sustainability Report
ASB’s approach to sustainability is shaped by our purpose of accelerating progress for all New Zealanders and is 
comprised of three interconnected strands: financial, social and environmental. As a bank we offer financial products 
and services, however we recognise we cannot accelerate progress for all New Zealanders unless we consider all three 
strands together. 
Supporting New Zealanders’ progress means focusing on doing the right thing and being transparent about our 
progress and performance. This report highlights some of the progress we’ve made this year towards supporting 
financial, social and environmental progress.  
How we prepare for and respond to climate-related risks and opportunities has been a focus for ASB this year, as 
presented through our climate statement in section 3 of this report. At ASB we acknowledge and respect the unique 
standing of Ma¯ori as Tangata Whenua of Aotearoa New Zealand and demonstrate this through our Te Ao Ma¯ori strategy. 
Pages 12-15 identify some of the actions we have taken this year to progress our Te Ao Ma¯ori strategy.

We consider strong governance an important element in supporting our purpose and strategy.  Environmental and social 
considerations are considered through our governance levels including ASB Board, our executive-level Environmental 
and Social Committee (ESC), and senior management Environmental and Social Action Group (ESAG). See pages 68-71 
to read more about governance at ASB.
ASB’s Environmental and Social (E&S) Framework recognises the interconnectedness of commercial, environmental, and 
social matters against the backdrop of changing community expectations. It sets our minimum environmental and social 
standards we seek to abide by and is underpinned by our internal E&S Policy. 
We review our E&S Framework annually and anticipate our six focus areas will evolve over time to reflect changing

In FY22 ASB engaged internal and external stakeholders to identify themes for our sustainability focus. In FY23 we 
reviewed these matters, but concluded they had not materially changed. 
To improve how we identify and focus our efforts in FY24 we have evolved our materiality process to ensure we are

undertaken a new multi-step materiality assessment alongside our strategy processes and stakeholder engagement.

Internal process to identify and theme topics

New Zealanders. 
•	 Issues were grouped based on similar themes. We considered our ability to influence them in relation  
to our social licence, history and connection to our existing operations.  
External materiality assessment 
•	 We engaged global market research firm IPSOS to undertake an external materiality assessment 
covering:
	
-	 Internal focus groups. 
	
-	 In-depth interviews with key external stakeholders to identify issues they consider ASB should 
prioritise.
	
-	 An online survey of 1,000 New Zealanders. 
Review of topics  
•	 The outcomes of our internal and external analysis were combined and top material topics were 
considered against ASB’s strategy and our ability to impact it.

•	 Our focus areas were identified and incorporated into our governance material and associated metrics 
identified.

About this climate statement
The Financial Sector (Climate-related Disclosures and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2021 was passed in 
October 2021 and it amended the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 (FMCA) to introduce a requirement for 
‘climate reporting entities’ to prepare climate statements in accordance with the climate-related disclosures 
(CRD) framework. It gave New Zealand’s External Reporting Board a mandate to develop the NZCS.
ASB is a climate reporting entity and is required to prepare climate-related disclosures in relation to the  
ASB Banking Group in accordance with the NZCS. A table of reference for NZCS requirements can be found on 
pages 92-95.

Strategy

Measuring our Financed Emissions 
To help our customers participate in and navigate a low-
emissions future, we need to understand our Financed 
Emissions. The term ‘Financed Emissions’ refers to 
emissions financed by lending and/or investments as 
per the Global GHG Accounting and Reporting Standard 
developed by the Partnership for Carbon Accounting 
Financials (PCAF Standard). Where possible we have 
aligned our approach with the PCAF Standard. Further 
detail on our Financed Emissions methodology and 
limitations of our estimations is detailed on pages 74-
81. We report Financed Emissions on our gross drawn 
lending balances at balance date and exclude invested 
emissions of our Managed Funds. 
Our modelling currently excludes finance and insurance, 
and government sectors due to data availability and 
materiality. The PCAF Standard does not have a 
methodology for consumer finance and assets held 
for short durations or designated as held for sale, 
consequently these amounts have been excluded in our 
estimations. We have also excluded Scope 3 emissions of 
our customers due to data limitations. 
We based our FY24 analysis on FY23 gross drawn lending 
balances, as customer and sector level data was not 
reported for FY24 at the time of our assessment. 
Progress on our Financed Emissions
In FY24 we have extended the calculation of Financed 
Emissions from business and home lending to also 
include the commercial real estate portfolio to cover 
96% of our drawn lending portfolio. 
Our absolute Financed Emissions have increased by 0.1 
megatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (MtCO2e) from 
FY22 to FY23 mostly driven by growth in our lending but 
also impacted by portfolio mix. Our emissions intensity 
has remained unchanged at 0.03 KgCO2e/$ lent.
The PCAF Standard applies a data quality score 
determined by the certainty of the data used. The data 
quality score is a scale from one (highest quality) to five 
(lowest quality). This year our PCAF data quality score 
for Dairy improved due to customer level emissions 
data being used where available. We aim to continue 
improving our data quality score over time as calculation 
methodology, quality and availability of customer-level 
data improves. 
Building our understanding of ASB’s Financed 
Emissions enables us to prioritise effort to develop 
targets to reduce Financed Emissions in sectors that 
contribute the most. We see this as an important first 
step in supporting our customers to transition to a 
low-emissions economy and working towards our 
commitment to progressively set sector-level Financed 
Emissions reduction targets on our lending portfolios.  
This year, we have prioritised and developed our first 
sector-level Financed Emissions intensity reduction 
target for our Dairy portfolio.6
Support Aotearoa New Zealand's transition to a low-
emissions and climate-resilient economy
Limitations and assumptions
Certain inputs to our calculation come from third parties. When using these inputs, we use the 
information that is at the Financed Emissions reporting period date or the closest period prior which is 
available. ASB has not independently audited or verified this third-party information.
To estimate our Financed Emissions, we generally allocate each loan to a specific sector. Where emissions 
intensity multipliers are used, we calculate the emissions for the customer based on their allocated 
sector. Accordingly, if a customer is diversified across business activities, the estimate of their emissions 
may be under or overstated. 
There are inherent uncertainties in the methodologies required to estimate Financed Emissions and data 
quality will be refined over time. Significant judgements due to lack of available data or our interpretation 
of the PCAF Standard have been further explained on pages 74-81.

Our Dairy sector target and portfolio
Our Dairy sector Financed Emissions intensity reduction 
target is focused on the reduction in financed biological

The Climate Change Commission (CCC) Demonstration 
Path has been used as a reference scenario for our Dairy 
sector Financed Emissions intensity reduction target. 
This scenario underpins CCC advice to the Government 
on Aotearoa New Zealand’s emissions budgets which 
set Aotearoa New Zealand on track to meet both 2030 
and 2050 emissions reduction targets and legislative 
requirements as part of the Climate Change Response 
Act 2002 (CCRA) to contribute to the global effort 
under the Paris Agreement to limit the global average 
temperature increase to 1.5° Celsius above pre-industrial 
levels.
Our Financed Emissions intensity reduction target is a 
useful metric to engage with our customers, as well as 
monitor our progress without the influence of portfolio 
lending shifts. Equally, we recognise that reducing total 
absolute emissions is the ultimate end goal as set out in 
the CCC advice to Government2. 
The Demonstration Path has been developed to reflect 
Aotearoa New Zealand’s unique emissions profile and 
provide a path to achieve Aotearoa New Zealand’s 
emissions budgets in a way that is fair, equitable and 
inclusive. Our Dairy sector Financed Emissions intensity 
reduction target does not currently rely on offsets.

Scenario analysis process
Introducing scenarios 
Climate scenario analysis is a process used to test the impacts from climate change on current systems, breaking down 
complex interrelationships of driving factors, to understand anticipated risks and opportunities. The findings are used to 
enhance risk management processes and can inform investment strategy. Scenario analysis constructs plausible future 
pathways, rather than a complete or certain view of the future, to challenge current thinking. 
ASB Banking Group scenario analysis process for FY24 
Over the course of the year, we built on our previous analysis reviewing climate-related risks under different scenarios to 
further our understanding of the key risks facing the ASB Banking Group. ASBGI is excluded from this scenario analysis 
process as it is a separate climate reporting entity.
Our process this year included a qualitative assessment of the key climate risks and opportunities facing the most 
material sectors of the Bank, over the time horizons which they may potentially materialise. Desk-based research was 
used to quantify potential impacts from the physical and transition impacts of climate change.
Our scenario analysis process
Scenario narratives used
Scenario narratives are projections of climate-related physical and transitional impacts describing the pathways 
to future events. The narratives used below describe the pathways to certain global temperature outcomes (1.5°C, 
>2°C, >3°C), and the events predicted to occur along the way. Although they are written with definitive language, 
they are only possible pathways of the future, not certain outcomes. Projections of climate impacts are limited by 
current scientific understanding of ecosystems and cascading influences on economies and society. Data availability 
is also limited, particularly in a New Zealand context. Outputs cannot be treated as statistically significant.
ASB's scenario narrative time horizons are aligned with the NZBA scenario narratives, and the temperature 
determined end points. ASB has chosen to consider short-, medium- and long-term horizons in analysis as there is 
meaningful differentiation in outcomes in these three periods and they broadly build on the timeframes considered 
in our strategy process. 
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) Stress Test scenario is similar to ASB's 2°C scenario narrative. As such it 
was also a source of information when deriving narratives and impacts. For more information on RBNZ Stress Test 
please refer to pages 58-59.
By using the NZBA sector scenarios as a basis to build ASB Banking Group specific narratives on, we believe the 
narratives used in our analysis retain the distinctive, consistent, and comparable qualities required of them. The 
NZBA scenarios were chosen as the baseline because they represent the most relevant downscaling, a process of 
applying global and national pathways to the New Zealand banking sector in which ASB Banking Group operates 
in. Through our downscaling process, ASB Banking Group has assessed that the narratives used are relevant to our 
business model and strategy, challenge our thinking and are plausible to the decision makers in our business. 
It is important to note that narratives and modelling may underestimate the impact of climate outcomes, including 
physical and transition risks.

•	 For our Rural lending portfolio, the potential for farmland to be submerged in water from flooding creates 
risks for pastures, soil quality, farm assets and the wellbeing of both the farmers and their animals.
•	 Extreme weather may directly impact the people and assets related to ASB's Corporate and Business 
Banking portfolios, including buildings, machinery, and other assets.
Short, medium 
and long-term
Heat stress and drought
As atmospheric temperatures increase, drought conditions and high temperature events are likely to become more 
severe and frequent. Drought conditions may negatively impact pasture and crop growth rates leading to reduced 
productivity, higher farm costs (feed substitutes) and lower meat prices (increased supply to market). 
Livestock animals’ physiological response to heat stress (high temperature and high humidity) may lead to reduced 
productivity and wellbeing. 
Some reduction in productivity expected in the short term, with regional increases in hot days expected to cause 
further reduction in the medium and long term.
•	 These events may negatively impact our Rural customers through reduced production and revenue as 
well as increased operating expenditure.
Medium and 
long-term
Sea level rise
Our Home Lending, Rural and Commercial Property lending portfolios are vulnerable to the impacts of sea level 
rise on real-estate. 
This risk is more likely to materialise in the medium to long term.
•	 Coastal flooding impacts on our residential and business lending have been considered in the RBNZ 
climate stress test detailed further on pages 58-59.
Transition risk
Short, medium 
and long-term
Insurance coverage, affordability and access
As improved climate modelling data becomes available, insurers will increasingly be able to identify high risk 
properties with greater accuracy. Insurers may take steps to reduce their risk exposure to properties in high-risk 
areas.
In the short term, insurers may increase premiums for higher risk areas and could cause insurance to become 
unaffordable to some customers or to underinsure. Insurers may also apply exclusions or even cease to provide 
insurance in the highest risk areas. While these changes to coverage are more likely to occur in the medium and long 
term, it is possible they could occur in the short term as well.
This risk exists across short, medium and long term. 
•	 Increases in the cost of insurance may reduce customers' ability to meet other financial obligations 
including servicing their mortgage.
•	 Risk-based changes to insurance pricing and coverage may impact market demand for property within 
higher-risk areas, reducing the value of security held by ASB in these areas.
Medium and 
long-term
Community-led retreat
New Zealand faces critical decisions relating to land use in the context of climate change, particularly where 
residential and industrial land is at risk of flooding, coastal erosion or other natural hazard risk. Costs of adaptation 
and community-led retreat may need to be borne by one or more of the following parties: Central Government, 
Local Government, insurers, banks, businesses, organisations or down to individuals or households. The Government 
has announced an intention to develop an adaptation framework setting out its approach to cost and information 
sharing. Any legislation required to support the framework is expected to be introduced in early 2025. 
This risk is more likely to materialise in the medium and long term.
•	 All these potential actions may impact market demand for property within higher risk areas and reduce 
the value of securities for ASB.

Quantitative analysis on climate-related risks
Quantitative analysis is useful to build understanding of specific climate-related risks by assessing relative financial

for our customers. Due to the selection of specific risks for quantification, as well as limitations in data and models, this

and anticipated impacts, to materialise. 
Physical risk exposure
For key physical risks identified in scenario analysis, 
ASB is developing management metrics to understand 
and monitor the risk. ASB’s metric analysis considers 
available data on hazards, exposure and vulnerability, 
to identify portfolio segments that may be exposed to 
elevated risk. 
Currently we use our physical risk data and analysis 
for portfolio monitoring, stress testing, and to inform 
management considerations of risk appetite.

Quantitative analysis uncertainties and limitations 
Climate change presents complex and interconnected risks with no simple solution. This creates a high level 
of uncertainty and limitations in quantifying financial impacts. Associated models and datasets are limited but 
developing at pace. Current quantitative analysis does not incorporate all aspects of climate risk, how risks may 
interact, or materialise in unexpected ways over longer time horizons. Future impacts are dependent on uncertain 
mitigation and adaptation efforts, which may change vulnerability over time. This analysis draws on the best 
information we have at the time when the analysis is performed.  
We intend to continue to develop and adapt our approach as more data and information becomes available.
What is ARI? 
Average Recurrence Interval, ARI, represents 
the scale of an event by probability of 
occurrence in any given year. Less properties 
are impacted in a 1-in-100 flood event, than 
a 1-in-500, but these events are predicted to 
occur more regularly. For example, there is a 
26% probability of a 1-in-100 event occurring 
within a 30-year term, compared with a 6% 
probability of a 1-in-500 event. The January 
2023 Auckland Anniversary Weekend 
flooding event was estimated to be at least a 
1-in-200 ARI in some locations.
Assumptions, uncertainties, and limitations are further outlined in Other Information on page 90.
Residential inland flood risk 
Floods are one of the most frequently occurring and 
damaging natural hazards in New Zealand. In FY23, 
scenario analysis identified inland flooding as the most 
significant physical risk hazard for residential properties 
in ASB’s home lending portfolio. 
In FY24 we estimated the present inland flooding risk 
for the majority of ASB’s home lending portfolio, using 
property-level estimated flood depth and expected 
building damage, sourced from Moody's RMS, for 
Average Recurrence Intervals (ARI) 1-in-100, 1-in-200, and 
1-in-500, under today’s climate conditions. 
Rural physical risk 
Climate change affects productive land, water supplies 
and other important resources and services that 
the rural sector relies on. From the scenario analysis 
process ASB identified drought, livestock heat stress, 
coastal inundation and inland flooding, as the most 
material climate-related physical risk hazards to ASB’s 
Rural lending portfolio (this portfolio comprises c. 9% 
of ASB total lending exposure).
To explore risks and opportunities further, ASB is 
developing a rural physical risk score to identify 
properties exposed to the four key hazards identified 
in scenario analysis, with analysis showing that 
drought and heat stress pose a greater challenge.
There is expected to be a geographic distribution of 
climate-related risks, with some regions experiencing a 
bigger change in risk than others, and many properties 
in ASB’s Rural lending portfolio are exposed to multiple 
of the climate hazards assessed. There are also 
opportunities for ASB and its customers to become 
more resilient to climate change.
While we have some understanding of the exposure 
of ASB’s Rural lending portfolio to physical hazards, 
understanding vulnerability is more challenging due 
to data limitations. Customers who have taken steps 
to adapt to physical risks may be more resilient than 
exposure data indicates. Considerations for existing 
or potential adaptation measures, such as water 
storage or shade for livestock, could reduce customer 
vulnerability. 
Please refer to pages 30-31 for more information on 
how we support our Rural customers.
We consider properties exposed when hazard data 
shows any level of floodwater at the property location. 
We estimate flood exposure for ASB's residential 
lending portfolio ranging from 13% for 1-in-100, to 
33% for 1-in-500 events as at 30 June 2024. It is 
important to note that real events are unlikely to 
impact all exposed properties to the same degree, due 
to localised differences in precipitation and property 
vulnerability.
Vulnerability could be reduced by factors such as floor 
height and building materials, which could influence the 
expected loss from flood damage. When considering 
these factors, using regional building assumptions, 
analysis indicates 0.4% (1-in-100) to 5% (1-in-500) of 
residential properties in our home lending portfolio 
could be vulnerable to expected damage greater than 
or equal to 0.5% of building replacement value.
A management metric has been developed to monitor 
the potential vulnerability of ASB’s home lending 
portfolio to inland flood risks. For more information, 
please see pages 64-65 and 90.
Insurance is currently the primary way to further 
reduce the risk of loss from flooding. To understand 
more about how we support our home lending 
customers, please see page 34.
See page 90 for further information on ASB's 
residential inland flood methodology.

Risk management
Integrating climate-related risk management into our 
overall risk management processes
At ASB, we recognise the importance of understanding not only climate-related risks themselves, but how these risks 
drive other financial, non-financial and strategic risks across our organisation. The frameworks and processes we use to 
identify, assess and manage these risks are integrated into our climate risk management approach and support ASB in 
continuing to understand the evolving E&S landscape and the risks posed by climate developments.
Risk Management Framework (RMF)
At ASB, risks are managed in accordance with the 
RMF. The framework is regularly reviewed to consider 
changes in best practice, the business operating 
environment and regulatory and community 
expectations.
The RMF defines how ASB identifies, evaluates and 
manages material risks. It articulates the risk system in 
place to adequately monitor and control ASB’s material 
risks and includes details on risk drivers, governing 
policies and committees, and key risk mitigations in 
place.  Additionally, it outlines Board and Management 
risk governance structure (see Governance section for 
further detail).  
The RMF is underpinned by ASB’s Three Lines 
of Accountability model that outlines roles and 
accountabilities for how risk is managed across ASB. 
The RMF is reviewed and approved by the Board on at 
least a triennial basis, or where required due to material 
changes in risk operating models or processes.
The RMF contains three critical components, all of which 
have integrated climate-related matters and risks into 
associated processes and artefacts: The ASB Group 
Risk Appetite Statement, the ASB Group Strategy and 
the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process. 
Climate-related risks are further integrated into ASB’s 
approach to risk management via other key processes 
that support the RMF as detailed in the ‘Identifying, 
assessing and managing climate-related risks’ section.
Risk Appetite Statement (RAS)
The RAS outlines the types and amounts of risk that the 
ASB Board is prepared to pursue or accept in our day-to-
day activities and in delivering on our strategic choices. 
Our risk appetite is reviewed, updated and approved by 
the ASB Board on an annual basis, and is set at a level 
which the Board expects management to operate in 
across all material risk types. ASB’s risk appetite is set 
based on reasonably foreseeable circumstances over 
the short term (1-3 years) however is not designed to 
accommodate more severe stressed scenarios. Our risk 
appetite is defined through both qualitative statements 
and quantitative indicators to measure performance 
against defined appetite for each risk type, and includes 
appetite settings and indicators for both climate-related 
physical and transition risks.
ASB Strategy Review
ASB refreshes its strategy annually. This includes how 
we respond to our operating environment, opportunities 
and risks, including climate change.  
Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process 
(ICAAP)
ICAAP is a dynamic and integrated process used 
by ASB to establish the appropriate level of capital 
required given its risk profile. As part of this process, 
climate change and the potential impact on ASB’s risk 
exposure profile is assessed and associated financial 
risks incorporated within ASB’s business strategy. The 
financial impact and likely time horizon of climate-
related financial risks materialising is informed by stress 
testing and scenario analysis and are considered by 
ASB’s capital plan. ASB’s ICAAP is a continuous process 
which is formally reviewed, documented and approved 
by Board on an annual basis.
Environmental and Social Framework
ASB’s E&S Framework publicly sets the minimum 
environmental and social standards we seek to abide 
by and is underpinned by our internal E&S Policy. 
Guiding principles that have informed the development 
of the E&S Framework and E&S Policy include taking 
a risk-based approach to environmental and social 
matters, seeking to mitigate environmental and social 
risks through dedicated products and services.

a source of strategic financial and non-financial risk 
for the Bank and it has the potential to impact the 
long-term financial wellbeing of Aotearoa. The E&S 
Framework details how we seek to address climate 
change.

Stress testing is a tool to identify and quantify potential risks under a stressed scenario. Results can be used to develop risk monitoring metrics and shape business decisions, with the goal of ensuring

In FY24 ASB completed the 2023 RBNZ Climate Stress Test. The scenario was titled 'Too Little, Too Late' and presented severe but plausible climate-related challenges spread over a 28-year period. 
The main purpose of this stress test was to test and improve banks’ capability in managing climate-related risks, and to identify risks to financial stability. ASB considered credit risk impacts to all 
material lending portfolios, operational risk to ASB properties and liquidity risk for the stressed scenario. A new stress testing model was built to achieve these requirements at a customer level 
over the 28-year period, which broadly aligns with the medium-term time horizon of the scenario analysis process. This model provides the capability to analyse some aspects of financial impacts of 
different scenarios in the future. 
Scenario analysis
Annually
Scenario analysis is a tool similar to stress testing, that is used to identify potential risks in a range of plausible futures. There are two main differences between stress testing and scenario analysis. 
Assumptions used in scenario analysis are generally more explorative than those used for stress tests. Secondly, both upside and downside scenarios are usually considered in scenario analysis, 
whereas stress testing usually models a single downside scenario. Overall, scenario analysis can provide additional information about a much wider range of outcomes, including identification of risk 
relationships between our lending portfolios or business model. Climate scenarios used by ASB are described in the Strategy section on pages 44-45. We intend to undertake scenario analysis on at 
least one sector on an annual basis.
Based on the elevated transition risk sectors as shown in the Strategy section on page 52, we included agriculture as well as home lending in our FY24 Scenario Analysis. These two sectors were 
the most material sectors from a Financed Emissions and a lending exposure perspective for ASB. ASB also included analysis of our operations in the process. Commercial Property and Sheep- Beef 
Cattle Farming were excluded from the FY24 Scenario Analysis. The time horizons used for scenario analysis are Short (<6 years), Medium (30 years), Long (50+ years).

Executive governance
The CEO has established the Environment and 
Social Committee (ESC). The ESC’s climate-related 
responsibilities, as set out in its charter, include 
oversight of compliance with the E&S Policy, of E&S 
strategies and of ASB's climate change programme.  
All members of the ASB Executive Leadership Team 
(ELT) are members of the ESC. 
In FY24, ESC met various times. The ESC, through 
management reports, provides information and/or 
recommendations to the ASB Board and direction 
back to the business units on climate-related matters. 
Please refer to Climate agenda items at our Board 
committees section for more information.
The ESC is supported by the ERC. The ERC 
oversees the operation of ASB’s frameworks for the 
management of risk and capital. The role of the ERC 
is to monitor and advise on material risks, including 
climate-related risks impacting ASB Banking Group, 
ASB’s RMF, ASB’s risk appetite and risk profile, 
the effectiveness of the compliance management 
framework impacting the material risk types, risk 
culture and behaviours and the internal control 
framework. All members of the ELT are members of 
the ERC, including the Chief Risk Officer. The ERC is 
chaired by the CEO.
In relation to climate change, the ERC provides risk 
governance oversight, challenge, and endorsement 
for the Group’s E&S commitments in line with the 
policy, standards, and associated delegations and E&S 
strategy. The ERC met various times in FY24.
Supporting governance 
The Environmental and Social Action Group (ESAG) is 
an advisory committee, responsible for advising ESC 
on E&S programmes of work, recommending material 
updates to the E&S Policy, overseeing and endorsing 
climate scenarios, and advising ESC on climate-related 
metrics and targets. Members of ESAG are senior 
ASB employees who have responsibilities for key E&S 
programmes of work. The ESAG meets monthly, or as 
otherwise determined by the ESAG Chair. 
Across ASB Banking Group, all senior leaders have a 
responsibility to build in E&S considerations, including 
climate change, to business decisions and interactions.
Board climate expertise
The ASB Board ensures that the appropriate skills 
and competencies are available to provide oversight 
of climate-related risks and opportunities through 
assessment of the collective Board capabilities at annual 
review and on the appointment of new directors.
ASB obtains an external independent performance 
evaluation of the ASB Board (including Board 
committees) at least once every three years, in 
addition to self-evaluation annually. The ASB Board 
also has an annually reviewed skills matrix which 
is updated as necessary following the annual self-
evaluation performance review. ESG capability is one 
of the governance capabilities assessed and recorded 
in the skills matrix. The 2024 external independent 
performance evaluation is currently being performed.
Non-executive directors are required to have significant 
experience across multiple skill areas. No director 
assumes responsibility for a single topic. The ASB Board 
collectively exercises its responsibilities. Directors are 
assessed as ‘high capability’ or ‘moderate capability’ on 
the key capabilities outlined in the skills matrix, based on 
their professional or non-executive experience relating 
to a capability. 
The ASB Board Chair, Dame Therese Walsh, is the 
Chair of Chapter Zero New Zealand. According to their 
website, the mission of Chapter Zero New Zealand is 
to mobilise, connect, educate and equip directors and 
boards to make climate-smart governance decisions, 
thereby creating long-term value for both shareholders 
and stakeholders.
The BRCC Chair, Dr Rod Carr, is the Chair of He Pou a 
Rangi Climate Change Commission (CCC). According to 
their website, the CCC's purpose is to guide Aotearoa 
New Zealand to change in ways that will help address 
the global problem of climate change. It provides 
independent, evidence-based advice to government on 
climate matters.
The ASB Board is responsible for overseeing continuing 
education opportunities for directors to develop and 
maintain the skills and knowledge required to perform 
their role. ASB has a continuing education programme 
incorporated into the ASB Board calendar which ensures 
that directors, individually and collectively, develop and 
maintain skills and knowledge. It is also expected that 
all directors continuously educate themselves to ensure 
they may appropriately and effectively perform their 
duties. Education undertaken by directors is recorded in 
the Directors’ Education Register. 
The ASB Board received an education session in March 
2024 on ASB management’s approach to climate and 
sustainability reporting. 
Board oversight of ASB’s strategy
The ASB Board is ultimately responsible for approving 
the ASB Banking Group strategy. As part of this the ASB 
Board considers climate-related risks and opportunities 
to provide guidance and oversight of ASB’s strategic 
plans.
The ASB Board approves the E&S Policy, which 
underpins ASB’s public E&S Framework. The E&S 
Framework sets the minimum environmental and social 
standards we seek to abide by, including for climate 
change. The E&S Policy is subject to regular review 
and was most recently reviewed by the ASB Board in 
September 2023. 
Climate metrics and targets 
The ASB Board sets and monitors progress of, and 
oversees performance against key metrics and targets 
for managing climate-related risks and opportunities, 
through reporting from ASB Management. This includes 
management and review of performance against ASB's 
strategy, including climate-related elements. 
In FY24 ASB Management reported to the ASB Board 
on progress of several material metrics and targets 
for managing climate-related risks and opportunities, 
for example ASB's Dairy sector Financed Emissions 
intensity reduction target and the Sustainability 
Funding Target. In November 2023, the ASB Board 
approved ASB's approach to the Dairy sector Financed 
Emissions intensity reduction target. A climate-related 
metrics paper was provided to ASB Board as part of 
Management’s E&S update in December 2023.
Executive remuneration 
ASB Bank’s executive performance and remuneration 
framework applies to the CEO and ELT.
Performance outcomes are based on what was achieved 
(scorecard assessment) and how it was achieved (values 
and risk modifier assessment), which informs variable 
remuneration outcomes. The scorecard consists of 
objectives and measures across Our team, Customer, 
Strategy, Risk and Financial Outcomes.
The Board introduced a new climate-related 
performance scorecard measure for FY24 for the 
CEO and ELT. 'Progress on climate change agenda' is 
one of the new objectives that forms part of the Risk 
and Financial outcomes category. The assessment of 
progress on climate change is both qualitative and 
quantitative informed by commentary and key climate 
change measures.

Assumptions, uncertainties and limitations
Climate risk analysis, guided by current information and 
understanding, involves uncertainties and limitations 
due to its reliance on modelling and assumptions 
about future conditions. Some of these uncertainties 
stem from modelling methods, assumptions about 
representation of the physical phenomena (hazards) 
within the model, the quality, completeness, and scale 
of the input data, the model’s resolution, as well as 
the interpretation of the modelling results.  As these 
uncertainties cascade through the complex modelling 
system, they can lead to potential underestimation or 
overestimation of the risk associated with a specific 
hazard.
Key assumptions in the home lending portfolio 
quantitative risk analysis include:
1.	 The risk assessed where property level risk data is 
available can be considered broadly representative of 
the portfolio.
2.	The use of regional vulnerability assumptions, where 
building characteristics are unknown.
Given the data limitations and modelling challenges, 
climate risk analysis must factor in the elevated levels 
of uncertainty in the decision-making process. As we 
rely on external climate data providers, readers of this 
climate statement should take note that the statements 
and judgements presented here may vary in the future. 
Home lending inland flooding methodology 
Inland flooding occurs when inland surface water 
(pluvial) and rivers (fluvial) overflow, submerging the 
land that is typically dry. This type of flooding can occur 
due to several factors, including intense precipitation, 
rapid snowpack melting, or when dams or levees fail.
•	 Flood Depth  - The RMS New Zealand Inland Flood HD 
Model captures sources of flood risk including pluvial 
and fluvial flooding, as well as flooding caused or 
exacerbated by snowmelt. The model simulates over 
350,000 inland flood events based on 50,000-year 
time series of simulated precipitation.  
•	 Damage Ratio (DR) - To convert hazard to damage 
for a given ARI, the vulnerability component in the 
RMS New Zealand Inland Flood model relates the 
amount of physical damage to buildings and contents 
to the severity of the flood at a property location. The 
model uses flood depth as a severity measure, and 
expresses the level of expected damage by the DR. 
The DR is defined as the ratio of the expected loss 
from flood damage (before any insurance terms are 
applied) to the replacement cost of an asset, such as a 
building and its contents.
The home lending inland flooding metric reflects DR 
greater than or equal to 0.5% in a 1-in-100 flood event.

Scenario analysis assumptions, uncertainties  
and limitations
The approach provides guidance, rather than a 
complete or certain view of the future. Projections 
of climate impacts are limited by current scientific 
understanding of ecosystems and cascading influences 
on economies and society. Data availability is also 
limited, and outputs cannot be treated as statistically 
significant. 
Since ASB's scenarios use the NZBA sector scenarios 
as the base, much of the limitations of our scenarios 
come from the limitations of the sector scenarios. The 
full description of these can be found in the NZBA 
scenario description, but the most relevant limitations 
to the ASB scenarios have been laid out below: 
•	 The sector scenarios map out different global 
and domestic climate, socio-economic, policy 
and technology pathways within the scenarios. 
The major limitation of this is that there can be 
differences between the global and domestic 
pathways for a common temperature outcome, due 
to calculation and modelling approaches as well as 
the way New Zealand may react. As such, ASB has 
preferred the domestic pathway parameters where 
relevant.  
•	 Climate drivers and impacts are evolving in 
magnitude and frequency in such a way scientists 
hadn’t predicted less than a decade ago. As 
such, there is an increased level of uncertainty in 
the assessment of these on ASB. Furthermore, 
tipping points in the physical and transition drivers 
are often subdued in severity, thus increasing 
the limitation of the numerical models. ASB 
has attempted to account for this through the 
qualitative analysis. 
•	 The data used to create these scenarios was 
sourced from RBNZ and NZBA retrieved as of 
1 June 2023. The publicly available data is likely 
to be updated in the future as new modelling and 
research is carried out. These updates may not align 
with the contents of ASB scenarios.
